spark.summary: Canary deployment routes a small, controlled slice of production traffic (e.g., 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%) to a new release while automated analysis compares its error rates, latency quantiles, and business metrics against the live baseline before promoting or rolling back.
spark.keyTakeaway: Progressive delivery limits blast radius to a tiny fraction of users, but only works if your traffic slice generates enough statistical sample size to detect regressions before full rollout.

concept.whyItMatters: Staging environments rarely replicate production data skew, cache hit ratios, or real client behavior. Canary deployments validate new code under authentic production traffic while capping initial exposure to 1%–5% of users, catching memory leaks, serialization bugs, and latency regressions before they cause a site-wide outage.
whenToUse: High-traffic services (>1,000 RPM) where a 1%–5% slice yields statistically meaningful sample sizes within a 5–15 minute bake step.
Algorithmic, ML-ranking, caching, or query-planner changes where subtle p99 latency or conversion regressions only surface under real production distributions.
Automated GitOps pipelines (Argo Rollouts, Flagger + Istio/Envoy) aiming for continuous, zero-touch promotion and automated rollback.
whenNotToUse: Low-traffic internal tools (<50 RPM) where a 1% canary receives less than 1 request every 2 minutes, making automated statistical comparison impossible.
Strict single-version compliance or embedded/air-gapped deployments where running two versions side-by-side is disallowed.
Breaking database schema changes where baseline and canary pods cannot safely read and write the same tables simultaneously.
keyPoints: Traffic splitting at L7 (Istio `VirtualService`, AWS ALB weighted target groups, NGINX Ingress) gives exact percentage control independent of pod replica count—unlike naive Kubernetes pod-ratio splitting.

Automated Canary Analysis (ACA) evaluates canary vs. baseline (or historical threshold) using non-parametric tests like Mann-Whitney U (used by Netflix Kayenta) on `http_5xx`, `p95/p99` latency, and saturation metrics.
Always check sample size: at 1% of 6,000 RPM (60 RPM = 300 requests in 5 minutes), a 0.5% error-rate regression produces only 1.5 extra errors, indistinguishable from noise.
Stateful or session-bound workflows should use header/cookie-based routing (e.g., `X-Canary: true` or consistent hashing on `user_id`) so a user does not bounce between v1 and v2 mid-checkout.
Every canary step must define hard abort criteria (e.g., `5xx > 1%` or `p99 > 450ms` for 2 consecutive 1-minute intervals) that immediately reset canary weight to 0%.

examples.title: Argo Rollouts + Istio Automated Canary for Search Ranking
examples.scenario: A search API handling 18,000 RPM deploys a new BM25+vector re-ranker using Argo Rollouts (`steps: [setWeight: 2, pause: 10m, setWeight: 10, pause: 15m, setWeight: 50, pause: 15m]`) backed by an `AnalysisTemplate` querying Prometheus.
examples.outcome: At 10% weight (1,800 RPM), Prometheus detects `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` jumping from 140ms to 390ms due to an unindexed filter. Argo aborts automatically in 90 seconds, restoring 100% traffic to baseline with 90% of users unaffected.

examples.title: Dogfooding + Header-Routed Canary for Mobile API v3
examples.scenario: Before exposing a new GraphQL schema resolver to external users, Envoy routes requests matching header `X-Employee-Tier: internal` (and 1% of anonymous mobile traffic via consistent `device_id` hash) to the canary Deployment.
examples.outcome: Internal engineers catch a null-pointer serialization edge case on legacy iOS payloads during the 2-hour dogfood phase before any external traffic weight increases.

tradeOffs.pro: Capping initial traffic at 1%–5% contains severe bugs to a tiny user cohort and enables automated abort.
tradeOffs.con: Multi-step bake windows (e.g., 10m + 15m + 15m) stretch total deploy time to 40–60 minutes, slowing hotfix urgency unless an emergency fast-path exists.

tradeOffs.factor: L7 Mesh Splitting vs. Replica-Count Splitting
tradeOffs.pro: L7 proxies (Istio/ALB) decouple traffic weight (e.g., 1%) from pod count (e.g., 1 pod out of 20), avoiding over-provisioning.
tradeOffs.con: Adds service-mesh or ingress controller configuration complexity and requires careful header/trace propagation (`version=canary`).

tradeOffs.pro: Comparing canary against a concurrent same-size baseline pod eliminates time-of-day traffic bias.
tradeOffs.con: Low-volume endpoints suffer high variance, causing false-positive rollbacks if thresholds are set too tightly.

failureModes.name: Insufficient Sample Size Masks Regressions
failureModes.description: Routing 1% of a 300 RPM service yields only 3 RPM to the canary; a 5% error rate produces ~1 error every 7 minutes, passing checks and exploding at 50%.
failureModes.mitigation: Either increase initial weight for low-RPM services (e.g., 10%), extend the bake window, or generate synthetic shadow traffic.

failureModes.name: Version Ping-Pong Breaks Multi-Step Sessions
failureModes.description: Random per-request 5% routing sends a user's `POST /cart` to v2 and `POST /checkout` to v1, failing on incompatible session state.
failureModes.mitigation: Use sticky consistent-hash routing on `user_id` or `session_id` cookie during the canary window.

failureModes.name: Missing Version Labels Pollute Baseline Metrics
failureModes.description: Prometheus alerts aggregate metrics by `service=orders` without `rollout_slot=canary|baseline`, averaging away a 10% error spike on a 5% canary.
failureModes.mitigation: Tag all Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry spans with `app.kubernetes.io/version` or `pod_template_hash` and query canary vs. baseline separately.

failureModes.name: Slow Memory Leak Passes Short Bake Windows
failureModes.description: A goroutine or heap leak takes 45 minutes to OOMKill pods, passing 5-minute canary steps and crashing the whole fleet an hour after 100% promotion.
failureModes.mitigation: Include memory slope (`deriv(container_memory_working_set_bytes[10m])`) in `AnalysisTemplate` and keep post-100% rollback automation active.

commonMistakes: Splitting traffic by Kubernetes ReplicaSet pod count (e.g., 1 canary pod + 9 stable pods = 10% minimum) instead of L7 weights.
Comparing canary p99 against yesterday's global average instead of a concurrent baseline pod under identical traffic.
Forgetting to include an emergency bypass flag (`--skip-analysis`) for urgent security or outage hotfixes.
Monitoring only HTTP 500s while ignoring business KPIs (checkout completion rate, empty-search rate) and saturation (CPU/heap slope).
Leaving old canary ReplicaSets or Istio VirtualService weights half-applied after a manual `kubectl` intervention.

sections.content:
## The idea

Canary deployment treats production rollout as a **controlled experiment** rather than an all-or-nothing switch. A new version deploys alongside the live baseline, receives a tiny initial slice of traffic (typically 1%–5%), and is continuously scored by an automated analyzer against golden signals (latency quantiles, 5xx error rate, saturation, and business conversion). Only if the canary matches or beats the baseline across each step does the router progressively shift traffic (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an Argo Rollouts pipeline for a payments-authorizer service running 20 baseline pods (`v4.1`) at 12,000 RPM:

1. **Canary Boot**: Pushing `v4.2` scales up 1 canary pod (`rollout_slot=canary`) while Istio `VirtualService` keeps `canary: 0%` until readiness probes pass.
2. **Step 1 (2% Weight, 10m)**: Istio shifts 2% (~240 RPM) to `v4.2`. Argo's `AnalysisTemplate` runs every 60 seconds, comparing `v4.2` against a dedicated 1-pod `baseline` (`v4.1`) so both have equal concurrency and cold/warm state.
3. **Statistical Check**: Prometheus queries `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",slot="canary"}[2m])` and `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)`.
4. **Step 2 & 3 (15% -> 50%)**: If error rate <= 0.5% and p99 <= 1.15x baseline for 10 consecutive checks, weight advances to 15% (1,800 RPM) and then 50% (6,000 RPM), scaling canary pods proportionally via HPA.
5. **Promote or Abort**: If any metric breaches threshold twice consecutively, Argo immediately sets `canary: 0%` in <5s and scales canary pods to 0. Otherwise, `v4.2` reaches 100% and replaces `v4.1`.

sections.content:
## Statistical confidence and shadow traffic

A common pitfall is running a 1% canary on low-QPS endpoints where random jitter triggers false alarms or hides real bugs. To detect a change from 0.2% to 1.0% error rate with 95% confidence and 80% power, each cohort needs roughly **1,500–2,000 requests**. At 500 RPM, a 1% canary (5 RPM) would take 5+ hours to reach significance. When traffic is too low for fast statistics, combine a small canary with **traffic shadowing (mirroring)** in Envoy (`mirror_percentage: 100%`), which replays live read-only requests asynchronously to v4.2 without impacting user responses.

## Canary analysis signals and thresholds

| Signal Category | Concrete Prometheus Metric | Typical Abort Gate | Why It Matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Availability** | `sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[2m]))` | `> 1.0%` or `> 2x baseline` | Catches unhandled exceptions, bad configs, serialization crashes |
| **Tail Latency** | `histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(..._bucket[2m]))` | `> 1.25x baseline` for 2 checks | Catches N+1 queries, lock contention, missing DB indexes |
| **Saturation** | `deriv(container_memory_working_set_bytes[10m])` | Positive monotonic slope > threshold | Catches slow memory/goroutine leaks before OOMKill |
| **Business KPI** | `rate(checkout_completed_total[5m]) / rate(cart_total[5m])` | `> 5%` relative drop vs baseline | Catches silent logic bugs returning HTTP 200 with empty/wrong data |

## Failure modes

1. **Sticky-Routing Skew**: Hashing on `IP` behind a corporate NAT routes 20% of all enterprise users into a "1%" canary. Hash on `user_id` or `session_id`.
2. **Asynchronous Side Effects in Shadowing**: Mirroring `POST /charge` requests causes double-billing unless mutating endpoints are excluded or idempotency-fenced.
3. **Baseline Drift**: Comparing a brand-new canary pod (cold cache, 10% CPU) against 20 warmed baseline pods skews p99; spin up 1 fresh `baseline` pod alongside the 1 `canary` pod for apples-to-apples ACA.

## Progressive delivery with feature flags

Canary deployments operate at the **infrastructure/binary** level, whereas feature flags (LaunchDarkly, OpenFeature) operate at the **code-path** level. Combining both gives maximum safety: deploy the binary via a fast canary (verifying runtime stability, memory, and p99 latency across 20 minutes), then progressively enable individual product features from 1% to 100% of targeted user segments via feature flags over days without redeploying containers.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use L7 weighted routing (Istio, Envoy, ALB) rather than Kubernetes pod-ratio splitting.
- [ ] Label all metrics, logs, and traces with `version` / `rollout_slot` (`canary` vs `baseline`).
- [ ] Verify minimum sample size per step (aim for >=1,500 requests per step before evaluating error rates).
- [ ] Use consistent hashing on `user_id` or session cookie for multi-step user flows.
- [ ] Include both technical golden signals (5xx, p99, memory slope) and at least one business success metric.
- [ ] Test an automated abort in staging by deploying a deliberately broken canary image.

interviewProblems.title: Zero-Downtime Continuous Deployment Pipeline
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are building the deployment engine for a global streaming service executing 100 production deployments daily across 5,000 Kubernetes pods. How do you design an automated Canary analysis and rollback pipeline?
constraints: Automatic rollback trigger latency under 10 seconds.

dimensions.name: Argo Rollouts & Traffic Weighting
dimensions.description: Using Service Mesh / NGINX ingress traffic weighting (2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%).

dimensions.name: Automated Metric Analysis & Rollback
dimensions.description: Comparing Prometheus error rates and p99 latency between canary and baseline.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use Argo Rollouts on Kubernetes with Istio service mesh traffic splitting. Shift 2% traffic to canary. Compare Prometheus HTTP 5xx rates against baseline pods every 60 seconds; trigger automatic rollback if errors breach 0.5%.
commonPitfalls: Deploying breaking database schema changes before code expansion phases.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Canary deployment routes a small, controlled slice of production traffic (e.g., 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%) to a new release while automated analysis compares its error rates, latency quantiles, and business metrics against the live baseline before promoting or rolling back.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Canary Fleet (v4.2) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Argo + Prometheus ACA.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Argo + Prometheus ACA experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Either increase initial weight for low-RPM services (e.g., 10%), extend the bake window, or generate synthetic shadow traffic.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Progressive delivery limits blast radius to a tiny fraction of users, but only works if your traffic slice generates enough statistical sample size to detect regressions before full rollout.
Avoid trap: Splitting traffic by Kubernetes ReplicaSet pod count (e.g., 1 canary pod + 9 stable pods = 10% minimum) instead of L7 weights.
Avoid trap: Comparing canary p99 against yesterday's global average instead of a concurrent baseline pod under identical traffic.
When to reach for it: High-traffic services (>1,000 RPM) where a 1%–5% slice yields statistically meaningful sample sizes within a 5–15 minute bake step.
When to reach for it: Algorithmic, ML-ranking, caching, or query-planner changes where subtle p99 latency or conversion regressions only surface under real production distributions.

putItTogether.title: Putting Canary Deployments Together
putItTogether.summary: Progressive delivery limits blast radius to a tiny fraction of users, but only works if your traffic slice generates enough statistical sample size to detect regressions before full rollout.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Canary Deployments before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: At 10% weight (1,800 RPM), Prometheus detects `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` jumping from 140ms to 390ms due to an unindexed filter. Argo aborts automatically in 90 seconds, restoring 100% traffic to baseline with 90% of users unaffected.
